subject: Purpose of Terraform state
description: Terraform state exists to bind objects that already exist in a remote system to the resource instances declared in configuration, so Terraform can determine what already exists without re-inspecting the real infrastructure on every run. This binding function is why state must be tracked accurately and shared across a team rather than reasoned about locally.

subject: Remote state for team collaboration
description: HashiCorp's own guidance is to store state in HCP Terraform or a remote backend rather than locally, specifically to secure it and allow team members to collaborate on the same infrastructure without passing state files around manually.

subject: State must not be stored in plain version control
description: Storing Terraform state in a version control system or any storage that lacks state locking and secure access control is explicitly discouraged, because it can cause data loss or expose secrets that end up embedded in the state file. [Stage 2 depth correction: reclassified from operation to judgment — see merge log.]

subject: State locking is automatic when supported
description: When the configured backend supports it, Terraform automatically locks state for any operation that could write to it, which prevents a second concurrent operation from acquiring the lock and corrupting state.

subject: Lock acquisition failure halts the run
description: If Terraform cannot acquire the state lock, it does not proceed with the operation at all — it stops rather than attempting to run unsafely against state someone else may be writing to.

subject: force-unlock risk of multiple writers
description: Terraform provides a force-unlock command for clearing a stuck lock, but HashiCorp's own docs warn that unlocking state while someone else genuinely holds the lock can result in multiple concurrent writers corrupting state — this is a judgment call about whether a lock is actually stale versus actively held. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-035 ("force-unlock on someone else's active lock can corrupt state"), which cited the identical quote from the same source. See merge log.]

subject: S3 backend native state-lockfile locking is opt-in, not automatic
description: State locking on the S3 backend is opt-in, not automatic, and as of current docs is implemented via a lockfile mechanism configured with the use_lockfile argument, distinct from the older DynamoDB-table-based approach. A team that copies a bare S3 backend block without adding either gets zero protection against concurrent writers and won't discover it until two applies collide. [Stage 2 depth correction: reclassified from mechanism to operation after merging a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-038, which cited the identical quote at depth operation. See merge log.]

subject: Health assessments never interrupt an active run
description: HCP Terraform's automated health assessments (which power drift detection) are designed to never block or interfere with a real plan/apply run — if a new run starts while an assessment is in progress, HCP Terraform cancels the assessment rather than the run.

subject: CLI workspaces hold multiple states per configuration
description: A Terraform backend starts with a single default workspace containing one state. Backends that support multiple named workspaces let more than one state be associated with the same configuration, which is the mechanism CLI workspaces use.

subject: Workspaces are unsuitable for environment/credential separation
description: HashiCorp explicitly states that CLI workspaces are not the right tool when you need to decompose systems or when different deployments require separate credentials and access controls — a common misuse at team scale is treating workspaces as environment isolation when they don't provide that isolation. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-040 ("Workspaces vs. separate directories for environment isolation"), which made the identical core claim — CLI workspaces share one backend and cannot isolate credentials/access across environments — citing an adjacent sentence from the CLI workspaces doc. See merge log.]

subject: Separate configurations are the documented alternative to workspaces
description: Rather than using CLI workspaces for distinct environments, HashiCorp's own CLI docs recommend building reusable modules for the shared logic and instantiating each environment as its own separate configuration pointed at a different backend — because workspaces within one working directory share a single backend and are therefore not an isolation mechanism for credentials.

subject: Modules should be opinionated and single-purpose
description: HashiCorp's module-creation pattern guidance says a good module does one thing well and is deliberately opinionated; if you struggle to explain what a module's purpose is, that itself signals the module has taken on too much complexity to be reusable.

subject: Module scoping: encapsulation, privilege, volatility
description: HashiCorp names three specific considerations for scoping a module for reuse: group infrastructure that is always deployed together (encapsulation), restrict a module to a single privilege boundary, and separate long-lived infrastructure from short-lived infrastructure (volatility) rather than mixing them in one module.

subject: Limit primary module nesting to two levels deep
description: As a general rule, primary modules should not be nested more than two levels deep, with an explicit exception carved out for small, common utility modules such as ones that just apply tags. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: the row's own depth_check names the consequence as 'module trees that are hard to reuse' -- a cost realized later, the judgment signature, not operation's 'breaks immediately and visibly.' A four-deep module tree plans and applies fine. Inconsistent as operation with sibling row T3-017 (thin-wrapper modules), which makes the same class of claim and is correctly judgment.]

subject: Keep the module tree flat; prefer composition over deep nesting
description: HashiCorp's module development guidance recommends keeping the overall module tree relatively flat and using module composition — combining sibling modules at the root rather than nesting modules inside modules — because flat, composed modules are easier to reuse in different combinations.

subject: Composition: modules receive dependencies rather than embedding them
description: In the composition pattern, a module does not create and manage its own private copy of a dependency; instead it receives that dependency as an input from the root module. This is what lets the same root module wire the same child modules together differently to produce different systems.

subject: Avoid thin-wrapper modules; raise the abstraction level
description: A well-designed module should introduce a new concept in your architecture built out of underlying provider resource types, rather than being a thin wrapper around a single resource type that adds no real abstraction.

subject: Dependency lock file remembers provider version decisions
description: After Terraform selects a specific version for each provider dependency, it records that decision in a dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) so that, by default, future `terraform init` runs reselect the same version instead of drifting to a newer one automatically.

subject: Commit the lock file so dependency changes go through code review
description: HashiCorp recommends committing the dependency lock file to version control specifically so that changes to external provider dependencies are visible and discussable in code review, the same way changes to configuration itself are reviewed — a direct lever for plan/apply review discipline at team scale.

subject: Standard CI/CD pipeline: init, plan, human review, apply
description: HashiCorp's automation guidance defines the core Terraform pipeline as four ordered steps: initialize the working directory, produce a plan, have a human operator review that plan for acceptability, and only then apply the changes described by the plan.

subject: Manual plan review is recommended whenever changes could be destructive
description: HashiCorp's own automation guidance states that manual review of a plan is always recommended when Terraform could make destructive changes to infrastructure, unless the team can tolerate downtime from an unintended change — auto-approval is not the default recommendation for anything where damage is possible.

subject: Saved plan files store sensitive data in cleartext
description: A saved Terraform plan file contains the full configuration, all planned values, and all plan options including input variables. If any of that data is sensitive — even if Terraform obscures it in terminal output — it is written to the plan file in cleartext, so saved plan files must be handled as sensitive artifacts (e.g., in CI/CD storage or artifact caches). [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: what a reader loses without this row is the knowledge that CI artifact retention is an access-control decision -- a choice made once whose failure is invisible at the moment it's made and surfaces only when the artifact store is later read by someone who shouldn't have access. That is judgment's late-surfacing signature, not operation's immediate one. Applied for consistency with T3-003, which Stage 2 already moved to judgment on the identical reasoning (Terraform writes secrets in cleartext, so control access to it).]

subject: A reviewed plan can go stale before apply runs
description: HashiCorp's docs warn that other changes to the target system made in the time between generating a speculative plan and actually applying it can cause the real effect of an apply to differ from what the earlier plan indicated — a direct risk for review workflows where plan and apply are separated in time.

subject: Static provider credentials are a risk even with rotation
description: HCP Terraform's own docs frame static credentials as a security risk in themselves, not just a risk when unrotated — the guidance explicitly states rotating static credentials regularly does not eliminate the risk, which is the stated motivation for using OIDC-based dynamic credentials instead. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-041 ("OIDC/dynamic credentials vs. static long-lived credentials"), which cited the identical quote. See merge log.]

subject: OIDC workload identity token generation
description: For dynamic provider credentials, HCP Terraform itself generates a workload identity token that conforms to the OpenID Connect (OIDC) standard and embeds metadata about the organization, workspace or Stack, and run stage — this token, not a stored secret, is what gets presented to the cloud platform to authenticate a run.

subject: Successful OIDC verification yields temporary credentials
description: After the cloud platform verifies the workload identity token against HCP Terraform's public signing key, it responds by returning a set of freshly generated temporary credentials for that run to use — no long-lived secret is ever provisioned into the run.

subject: Temporary OIDC credentials are discarded when the run ends
description: Once a plan or apply run completes, HCP Terraform tears down the run environment and discards the temporary credentials that were issued for it, so no reusable long-lived credential persists after the run finishes.

subject: Drift detection runs as periodic refresh-only plans
description: HCP Terraform's drift detection works by determining whether real-world infrastructure still matches the Terraform configuration, implemented as periodic health assessments that run non-actionable, refresh-only plans against the workspace's tracked state without changing infrastructure or state themselves. [VERIFY gap, caught by 3B in passing / missed by 3A: the stored quote ("Drift detection determines whether your real-world infrastructure matches your Terraform configuration") supports only the row's first clause. The mechanism detail appended to it -- "implemented as periodic health assessments that run non-actionable, refresh-only plans against the workspace's tracked state without changing infrastructure or state themselves" -- is not in the stored quote and was not independently verified this stage. Recorded as a real gap in the Haiku verify pass: a partial quote that only covers the easy half of a two-clause claim.]

subject: Dependency graph: resource meta-nodes represent count expansion
description: In Terraform's internal dependency graph, a resource meta-node does not represent an action on its own — it exists only to represent a group of resources, and only appears when a resource block has a count parameter greater than one, standing in for the set of expanded instances. [ABSENCE (3B) note, no grade change: dependency-graph count-expansion meta-nodes are not clearly inside the declared boundary (remote state, module design, multi-env CI/CD, workspaces, OIDC, drift, plan/apply review) -- flagged as a scope-drift observation, not a defect. Also cites developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/graph, which may describe a pre-current graph model; not independently re-verified this run.]

subject: Graph execution runs concurrently, not strictly sequentially
description: Terraform does not walk its dependency graph one node at a time by default — up to 10 nodes are processed concurrently as their dependencies are satisfied, and this concurrency limit is configurable via the -parallelism flag, which explains why plan/apply operations on independent resources can interleave.

subject: State file contents are sensitive by default
description: Terraform's state file stores a JSON snapshot of every managed resource, including secrets, passwords, and other sensitive attribute values in plaintext, so it must be treated as sensitive data with restricted access and encrypted, versioned remote storage - not committed to source control or left world-readable in a bucket. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: identical reasoning to T3-022 and T3-003 -- three rows making one claim ('Terraform writes your secrets somewhere in cleartext, so control access to it') should not sit at two different depths. T3-003 was already moved to judgment by Stage 2 on this exact reasoning.]

subject: Provider/Terraform version bumps cascade through every module
description: Because each module pins or inherits its own required_providers and required_version constraints, upgrading the Terraform CLI or a provider version for a team's codebase means walking every module that uses it and bumping its constraint too - teams that treat this as a one-line change get blocked mid-upgrade by a module several layers down still pinned to the old version.

subject: Switching a resource from count to for_each rebuilds it
description: Changing a resource or module call's meta-argument from count to for_each changes its state address from a numeric index (e.g. [1]) to a string key (e.g. ["1"]); Terraform treats these as different objects, so the plan shows the old instance destroyed and a new one created rather than an in-place rename, unless a moved block tells Terraform they're the same object. [VERIFY gap, caught by 3B in passing / missed by 3A: the stored quote is a GitHub issue TITLE phrased as a question ("When I change count to for_each, the resource will rebuild ?"), not an assertive statement -- it does not itself support the row's factual claims about state addressing and destroy/recreate behavior. The underlying claim is very likely true (it matches Terraform's documented addressing model) but the quote as stored fails the v0.3 contract: a quote that cannot support its claim signals the claim needs a better source or authored-with-inference labeling, per the Stage 1B brief. 3A's mechanical quote-check should have caught this and did not -- recorded as a real gap in the Haiku verify pass, not a false alarm.]

subject: Read-only Terraform commands can still block on a held state lock
description: HashiCorp's documentation says Terraform locks state "for all operations that could write state," but the etcdv3 backend locked on pure read operations like terraform state list and terraform show too, contradicting that description and blocking teammates from even inspecting state while a lock was held elsewhere; HashiCorp closed the report as not planned rather than aligning the backend's behavior.

subject: -lock=false silently removes the concurrency safety net
description: Most Terraform commands accept -lock=false to skip acquiring the state lock; it's offered as an escape hatch for a stuck pipeline, but HashiCorp's own documentation explicitly recommends against it because it reopens the exact concurrent-write risk locking exists to prevent. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment, for consistency: T3-006 (force-unlock on a held lock -> multiple writers) and this row (-lock=false -> the same multiple-writer hazard) cite the same doc page about the same hazard and had landed at different levels. -lock=false runs successfully; the concurrent-write damage surfaces later, which is judgment. T3-006 was the correctly-assigned one.]

subject: An out-of-sync plan applied late causes mass unintended deletion
description: GitLab's July 2023 site-wide outage was caused by executing a Terraform plan generated three weeks earlier; in the interim, real infrastructure drifted from what the plan assumed, so applying the stale plan removed and replaced 617 production resources instead of performing the intended database upgrade. [VERIFY (3A, Haiku) viable->wounded: the stored quote supports only the general claim ("an out-of-sync infrastructure configuration plan executed against production"), not the specific '617 production resources' figure the description states. Re-fetched the GitLab incident page, which does contain '617 resources to be destroyed' -- so the underlying fact is true, but the quote as stored does not carry it, which is exactly the failure mode Change 1 is meant to make visible.]

subject: A shared module with its own provider block can't be called with count/for_each/depends_on
description: A module meant to be called by other modules must not define its own provider blocks; if it does, Terraform rejects using that module call with the for_each, count, or depends_on meta-arguments, because provider configurations are global to the whole configuration and can't be parameterized per-instance the way those arguments imply.

subject: Reviewing plan output, not just HCL diffs, before merge
description: For a team, the value of terraform plan is as a review artifact, not just a preview: pairing plan output with the pull request lets reviewers see exactly what will change, ask questions, and catch mistakes that reading the HCL diff alone would miss, since HCL changes and their real infrastructure effects aren't always obvious from the code.

subject: Scoping state/workspace boundaries to limit blast radius
description: Because any write operation against a state file can affect every resource tracked in it, HCP Terraform's own guidance is to keep each workspace's state small and scoped to logically related resources rather than grouping unrelated infrastructure (e.g. compute and database) into one state file - the state boundary is a risk-containment decision, not just an organizational convenience.

subject: HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate (004) learning path
description: HashiCorp's own guided study path for the Terraform Associate 004 exam, linking directly to official tutorials covering state management (remote state, locking, drift), module creation and reuse, and HCP Terraform workspaces/CI integration, ordered by exam objective rather than as a single article.

subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Module creation - recommended pattern
description: Official hands-on HashiCorp tutorial that walks through scoping a three-tier web application into six separate reusable modules (network, web, app, database, routing, security), applying encapsulation/privilege/volatility criteria to decide module boundaries, then documenting them for other teams to consume.

subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Automate Terraform with GitHub Actions
description: Official hands-on tutorial building a two-workflow GitHub Actions pipeline against an HCP Terraform workspace: one workflow generates a speculative plan on every pull request for review, the other applies on merge to main, using HashiCorp's own tfc-workflows-github actions and a real HCP Terraform team token.

subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Authenticate providers with dynamic credentials
description: Official hands-on tutorial that has the reader establish a trust relationship between HCP Terraform and a cloud provider, then configure a workspace to receive short-lived, run-scoped credentials via OIDC instead of static access keys.

subject: Terraform Associate practice exercises (state, modules, meta-arguments)
description: A third-party GitHub Pages set of six hands-on exercises for Terraform Associate prep covering AWS/GCP: first configuration, variables/outputs, resource dependencies, working with state (remote state and state locking), modules (creation/versioning/registry), and meta-arguments (count, for_each, lifecycle, dynamic blocks). Each exercise directory includes a README and a working solution.

subject: Drill: reproduce and recover from a state lock collision
description: Stand up a local backend or a scratch S3 bucket without locking enabled and run two overlapping `terraform apply` processes against the same state to observe a corrupted or conflicting write. Reconfigure the backend with locking on (e.g. S3's use_lockfile) and repeat, observing the second run correctly blocked with a lock-acquisition error instead. Finally, kill the first process mid-run to leave a stale lock, and practice diagnosing from the lock info (who holds it, since when) whether it is actually safe to force-unlock before running that command — the judgment call the cluster's sources (T3-006, T3-035) warn is easy to get wrong under pressure.

subject: Drill: refactor a mega-module into scoped, composed modules
description: Take a single flat root configuration that manages several unrelated pieces of infrastructure as one module (e.g. a VPC, a compute service, and a database). Split it into separate modules scoped by HashiCorp's own encapsulation, privilege, and volatility criteria (T3-013); wire them together via composition, with the root module passing outputs as inputs rather than any module embedding its own provider or a dependency it doesn't own (T3-016); keep nesting to no more than two levels (T3-014); and audit the result for thin-wrapper modules — any module that is just one resource with no real abstraction — eliminating or merging them (T3-017).

subject: Drill: build a plan-on-PR/apply-on-merge pipeline with OIDC auth and a mandatory human-review gate
description: Wire a CI pipeline (e.g. GitHub Actions) that runs `terraform plan` on every pull request and posts the plan output itself — not just the HCL diff — as a reviewable PR artifact (T3-042), gates `apply` behind required human approval whenever the plan shows a destructive change (T3-021), and authenticates to the cloud provider via short-lived OIDC-issued credentials rather than static keys (T3-024–T3-027). Handle the saved plan file as a sensitive artifact, since it contains cleartext values (T3-022). Then deliberately let a plan go stale — approve it, make an out-of-band change to the target resource, and try to apply the old plan — to feel firsthand why HashiCorp and the GitLab postmortem (T3-023, T3-037) both treat plan staleness as a live risk rather than a theoretical one.

subject: Drill: convert an environment-by-CLI-workspace setup into separate configurations per environment
description: Start with a single root module and use `terraform workspace new` to create dev/staging/prod workspaces against one shared backend and one set of provider credentials. Identify concretely what this setup cannot do — scope IAM permissions differently per environment, or isolate one environment's state operations from another's (T3-010) — then refactor into separate per-environment root configurations, each with its own backend key and credentials, sharing common logic through a reusable child module (T3-011), exactly as HashiCorp's own CLI docs recommend as the alternative to workspaces.

subject: Drill: manually induce and detect infrastructure drift
description: Apply a small Terraform-managed resource, then modify it out-of-band — through the cloud console or CLI, not through Terraform — so its real state diverges from configuration. Run `terraform plan` and confirm it correctly reports the drift as a diff to reconcile (T3-028). If using HCP Terraform, configure a scheduled health assessment on the workspace, trigger a run while an assessment happens to be in progress, and confirm the assessment is what gets cancelled, not the run (T3-008) — the non-obvious ordering the drift-detection docs specify.

subject: Drill: intentionally break and repair a multi-module provider-version upgrade
description: In a repo with at least two modules that each declare their own required_providers constraints, bump the provider version constraint in only the root module and run `terraform init` — observe it fail or resolve inconsistently because the child modules are still pinned to the old constraint (T3-032). Commit the resulting `.terraform.lock.hcl` change and practice reading a lock-file diff the way a PR reviewer would (T3-018, T3-019). Then correctly walk every module, bump each constraint in turn, and re-run `init` to confirm the lock file re-resolves cleanly across the whole tree.

subject: Reading another configuration's state with terraform_remote_state
description: The terraform_remote_state data source reads the latest state snapshot from another configuration's backend and exposes that configuration's root module output values to the caller. This is the mechanism that makes state decomposition workable: once a team follows the harvest's own advice to split state for blast-radius containment (T3-043) and to give each environment its own configuration and backend (T3-011), the separated configurations still need to reference each other's outputs, and this data source is the documented way to do it. The same page notes that only root-level output values are exposed -- resource data and nested-module outputs are not.

subject: Reading another team's outputs grants read access to their entire state snapshot
description: Granting a configuration access to another configuration's outputs via terraform_remote_state is not a narrow permission. The state snapshot is a single object in the backend, so any principal with enough access to read the root module output values can also read the full state snapshot by direct network requests. Combined with the fact that state stores secrets in plaintext (T3-031, T3-003), this means the decision to let team B consume team A's remote state is a decision to let team B read every secret in team A's infrastructure. HashiCorp's own docs recommend a separately published data store for cross-team values where that is not acceptable.

subject: required_version pins the Terraform CLI version for a configuration
description: The terraform block's required_version setting specifies which versions of the Terraform CLI are allowed to run the configuration, and Terraform prints an error and exits without taking any action when the running CLI does not satisfy the constraint. This is the third and outermost level of version pinning at team scale -- distinct from provider constraints and from the dependency lock file, which the same docs note applies only to the CLI itself and not to provider plugins. Without it, engineers and CI runners on different CLI versions can produce different plans and, worse, a newer CLI can write a state format an older CLI cannot read.

subject: Pin external module versions with the version argument
description: HashiCorp recommends explicitly constraining the acceptable version numbers of every external module call, to avoid unexpected or unwanted changes. The same page states the version argument is only usable when the module's source points to a registry (the public Terraform Registry or a private registry); local-path modules do not support it because they share their caller's version, and for other source types (notably git) the pin has to be expressed in the source string itself. This is the second of the three pinning levels a team needs and is not covered by any provider-level mechanism.

subject: The dependency lock file never locks module versions
description: The dependency lock file tracks only provider dependencies. Terraform does not remember version selections for remote modules at all; on every init it reselects the newest available module version that satisfies the stated constraint. A team that commits .terraform.lock.hcl and concludes it now has reproducible builds is half right: providers are pinned, modules are not, and an unpinned or loosely-pinned module source will silently change between a plan run on a developer's machine and an init in CI with the identical committed lock file. This is the exact reason the module version argument (T3-058) cannot be skipped just because the lock file is committed.

subject: Applying a saved plan file is unprompted; passing the file is the approval
description: The pipeline shape in T3-020 (init, plan, human review, apply) is only sound if apply consumes the reviewed artifact rather than recomputing one. Terraform supports this by writing a plan to a file with plan -out=FILE and applying that file directly, and when a saved plan file is passed to terraform apply, Terraform performs the operations in that saved plan without prompting for confirmation -- the docs state that passing the plan file is itself interpreted as the approval. This is the operational rule that makes plan/apply review discipline mean anything, and it is also why a stale saved plan executes with no second gate in front of it (see T3-023 and the GitLab incident in T3-037): the approval was captured weeks earlier, at plan time.

subject: Drift detection without HCP Terraform: plan -detailed-exitcode
description: Every drift-detection row in this set (T3-008, T3-028) describes HCP Terraform health assessments, which a team not on HCP Terraform cannot use. The open-source equivalent is terraform plan -detailed-exitcode, which changes the command's exit codes so a scheduled job can distinguish outcomes programmatically: 0 means succeeded with an empty diff, 1 means error, and 2 means succeeded with a non-empty diff, i.e. drift or pending changes. Exit code 2 is what a cron job or CI schedule alerts on. Without this, a scripted drift check has to parse human-readable plan output, which is not a stable interface.

subject: OIDC to a cloud provider is available in ordinary CI, not only HCP Terraform
description: All six OIDC rows in this set (T3-024 through T3-027, T3-041, T3-047) describe HCP Terraform's dynamic provider credentials, which leaves a reader with the false impression that the alternative to static keys is a HashiCorp product. The same trust exchange is available to a plain CI runner: GitHub Actions workflows can access cloud resources without storing any credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets, by requesting a signed OIDC token from GitHub, presenting it to the cloud provider, and receiving a short-lived access token scoped to that job run. For a team running Terraform in GitHub Actions against an S3 or GCS backend -- the most common non-HCP setup -- this, not HCP Terraform, is how the judgment in T3-024 actually gets implemented.
